cards.title: Non-obvious-but-true framework for campaign ideas
cards.summary: Generate marketing stunts and campaigns by filtering out any idea that is obvious; only non-obvious ideas that are also true can move the needle.
cards.use_when: You are brainstorming a launch stunt, viral campaign or brand moment and need a filter to kill cliché ideas fast.

cards.title: Launch playbook: pre-seed anticipation, sampling and email list
cards.summary: Sequence a product launch by seeding anticipation months ahead, running aggressive free-sample campaigns and building a pre-launch email list to convert on day one.
cards.use_when: You are planning a new product or brand launch and want to engineer a large first-week sales surge.

cards.title: Sampling and generosity as a growth line item
cards.summary: Treat free product given to customers and creators as a fixed P&L line rather than a tracked ad channel, because the LTV math and generosity-driven word of mouth outperform pure paid spend.
cards.use_when: You are deciding how to allocate marketing budget between paid ads and free product/trial, or setting up an influencer seeding program.

cards.title: Gross margin must include final-mile, 3PL and transaction costs
cards.summary: True gross margin for a CPG/DTC brand must factor in shipping, 3PL and transaction fees, and the source treats 40–50% as the viable threshold.
cards.use_when: You are pricing a product or evaluating unit economics before launch, or deciding whether a category can support DTC plus retail.

cards.title: Brand vs performance marketing sequencing by lifecycle stage
cards.summary: Shift budget from mostly performance marketing early to mostly brand marketing as distribution and household penetration grow, because brand raises the tide across all channels.
cards.use_when: You are setting your paid-vs-brand budget split for a store in early growth versus a scaled omni-channel business.

cards.title: Packaging: brand-first, flavor-second inverse hierarchy
cards.summary: Invert the category convention of flavor-color-first branding by leading with a single strong brand color and communicating flavor second, borrowing from pre-natural-era packaging like Reese's.
cards.use_when: You are designing or redesigning packaging/on-shelf presence and deciding hierarchy between brand identity and flavor communication.

cards.title: Redirecting a small brand's pitch to value-laden language
cards.summary: When you're in 'protein no man's land' with a confusing name, use ingredient-led, value-loaded copy instead of generic claims to communicate differentiation.
cards.use_when: Your product's name or category positioning is confusing and standard claims (e.g. '12 grams of protein') don't differentiate you on the PDP or packaging.

cards.title: Briefing a creative agency with real direction
cards.summary: Give a creative agency a detailed, tension-filled brief with your strategic variables rather than a vague 'go make something,' because a bad creative outcome is your responsibility, not the agency's.
cards.use_when: You are commissioning packaging, a brand identity or a campaign and deciding what to put in the brief.

cards.title: Gender tension in brand design
cards.summary: Use deliberate masculine/feminine tension in naming and color to widen appeal, because men avoid feminine-coded products while women will adopt masculine-coded ones when beautiful.
cards.use_when: You are naming or designing a brand and deciding whether to aim at one gender or straddle both to widen market.

cards.title: Positioning on facts, not diet trends
cards.summary: Build brand positioning around durable facts (protein, calories) instead of riding a diet trend like paleo, which leaves you vulnerable when the trend fades.
cards.use_when: You are choosing messaging and category positioning for a food, supplement or wellness product, and deciding which claims to lead with.

cards.title: Honest reframe of dietary myths for retail feed
cards.summary: When a nutrition trend is proven wrong, use the correction as a positioning opportunity by reframing the product around more legible, true nutrition principles.
cards.use_when: You sell bars or supplements and are deciding how to update claims/messaging after a diet fad fades in your category.

cards.title: Trade-show decision: attend only if buyer access is the goal
cards.summary: Skip or attend trade shows by reasoning from the objective — if the goal is meeting category buyers and you already have retailer relationships, the cost may not be worth it.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to invest budget and team energy in a trade show or expo for retailer distribution.

cards.title: Creator/celebrity credibility strategy for nutrition brands
cards.summary: Choose credibility partners rooted in facts and nutrition thought leadership rather than athletes, and consider under-the-radar specialists as the current arbitrage.
cards.use_when: You are selecting influencers, celebrity partners or affiliates for a food/supplement/e-commerce brand and deciding who is worth the cost.

cards.title: Viral crisis response method (mean-girls style)
cards.summary: When an unrelated scandal or viral attack hits, run a fast war-room response rather than a slow legal-first process, because timing and content speed determine whether you control the narrative.
cards.use_when: Your brand is pulled into a viral moment, controversy or social pile-on and you must decide how fast and how to respond.

cards.title: Fix a Confusing Brand Name With Package Design Instead of a Rebrand
cards.summary: When the brand name doesn't communicate the product, solve it with packaging design and value-language rather than an expensive rebrand.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to rename/rebrand a product or rework the packaging/PDP hierarchy instead.

cards.title: Communicate Protein in Consumer Value Terms, Not Marketing Metrics
cards.summary: Translate an ingredient or protein claim into something shoppers already value (three egg whites) instead of an abstract gram number.
cards.use_when: Writing hero copy, packaging hierarchy or ad creative for a supplement, snack or food product where the protein/ingredient claim is generic.

cards.title: Retail Rollout: Build Distribution Blocks Before Mass Retail
cards.summary: Onboard retail distribution in high-confidence bites — specialty or regionally confined chains first — so you can support and service the volume before negotiating with mass retail.
cards.use_when: Planning physical retail distribution expansion or evaluating a mass-retail (Walmart/Target) offer for a young brand.

cards.title: Use Geographic Concentration to Stack Marketing Against Retail Doors
cards.summary: Concentrate retail distribution in one geography so all marketing tactics — digital, out-of-home, local creators — compound on the same audience.
cards.use_when: Choosing which retail chain or region to launch with, or deciding where to point paid and creator spend.

cards.title: Define a Specific ICP, Then Watch for a Broader Later Cohort
cards.summary: For the initial stage, define your customer narrowly (sub-12%-body-fat CrossFit four-times-a-week); only broaden your segment definitions when the founding niche is big enough or you can still find a correlated buying signal.
cards.use_when: Choosing which audience to speak to in creative and product launch positioning, before the brand has broad awareness.

cards.title: Ride a Fitness Trend via Its Dominant Skill, Not Its Name
cards.summary: When a trend like CrossFit or Hyrox emerges, build the product around the specific high-value skill/behavior (e.g. running) and invest in the community, rather than anchoring the brand to the trend's name.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether to sponsor, co-brand or build a product line for a fast-growing fitness community.

cards.title: Mind the Novice-to-Movement Dilemma Before a Mass Channel Launch
cards.summary: Fads and fitness/diet movements create demand but also risk if the brand's product is not made for the mass retailer's shopper or price expectations (the 'innovator's dilemma' in food).
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to enter a mass retail channel or a new product category tied to a temporary movement.

cards.title: Improve the Product Even When It Raises COGS
cards.summary: Switching to a materially better input can be a better decision than protecting gross margin, because the product drives stickiness.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to absorb a cost increase for a better ingredient or component in your hero product.

cards.title: Map Single-Source Vendor Dependencies and Treat Vendor Relations as Mutualism
cards.summary: Scan your business for dependencies like a single manufacturer, mitigate them, and run vendor relationships as reciprocal mutualism rather than leverage.
cards.use_when: Reviewing supply chain risk per SKU or renegotiating manufacturing, ingredient, or fulfillment vendor contracts.

cards.title: Run a Competitive Sell-Side Process and Sell the Company Yourself
cards.summary: Investment bankers run the process, but the CEO sells the company; a good process is designed, timed, competitive and transparent.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to sell the business, preparing for a sale process, or preparing to raise investor capital.

cards.title: Use an IPO/House Analogy to Structure the Company and the Story for a Sale
cards.summary: Prepare the whole company to be bought — not just do the deal — by auditing accounting, reporting speed and every function so buyers can underwrite the existing business and the easy growth.
cards.use_when: Preparing your business for a future sale or making the company more survivable during rapid growth.

cards.title: Run Founder, CEO and Shareholder Roles Separately to Protect Company Behavior Through a Sale
cards.summary: Separate your roles as founder, CEO-employee and shareholder so you handle the emotional and operational sides of a sale without over-celebrating or leaving the business hanging.
cards.use_when: Navigating a company sale or major exit while continuing to run the organization.

cards.title: Scale Servant Leadership by Teaching Agency Instead of Solving Everything
cards.summary: Servant leadership improves small teams but can create dependency and destroy agency at scale; great leaders move between micromanaging and delegating and preserve the best-idea meritocracy.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why decisions bottleneck on you as the team grows, or reconsidering how much you intervene in day-to-day work.

cards.title: Method: Forecast the Three Numbers That Matter in an Inventory-Heavy Business
cards.summary: Track inventory (raw and finished), net revenue, and cost of goods as the core metrics of an inventory-heavy CPG business; inventory is cash.
cards.use_when: Building a weekly reporting dashboard, diagnosing supply issues, or setting up forecasts for an inventory-heavy ecommerce or CPG operation.

cards.title: Use Consumer Surplus to Evaluate New Product Concepts
cards.summary: Define the consumer surplus as what people are willing to pay for the benefit minus what you charge, and use it as the core product-development test.
cards.use_when: Choosing products or SKUs to launch, or formulating a pricing and positioning strategy against existing substitutes.

cards.title: Decide International Expansion Only After Reaching Scale in the U.S.
cards.summary: The source treats the U.S. as the best and only food market that matters for now, requiring scale and 'boredom' before adding international complexity.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to open international storefronts, distributors or shipping for a growing consumer brand.

cards.title: Don't Emulate Fast Followers or Perfume the Pig in a Sale
cards.summary: Fast followers rarely win in category creation, and in a sale process the buyer will find out everything, so transparency beats trying to present a perfect story.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to copy a category leader's product, or preparing for buyer diligence and disclosure in a business sale.

cards.title: Price Against Consumer Surplus, Not Cost
cards.summary: Value your product by what customers would actually pay versus your price, and protect the delta as surplus.
cards.use_when: Setting or defending product pricing and evaluating whether a new SKU has room to launch at a premium.

cards.title: Back Macro-Nutrient or Benefit Bets Over Diet Fads
cards.summary: Bet product lines on durable macronutrients and universal benefits rather than elimination diet trends.
cards.use_when: Deciding which category to build a product line in and whether a health trend is durable enough to justify inventory and development.

cards.title: Find Contrarian Ingredients With Bad Branding
cards.summary: Ingredient reputation can diverge from its actual merit, creating a contrarian product opening.
cards.use_when: Sourcing or formulating a product and looking for an under-valued input with a mispriced reputation.

cards.title: Observe Shoppers in Convenience and C-Store Contexts
cards.summary: Direct observation of buyers in c-store aisles reveals behavior surveys cannot capture.
cards.use_when: Doing customer research for product packaging, shelf placement, or packaging design decisions.

cards.title: Run the Business Capital-Efficiently Before Raising
cards.summary: Strong P&L and self-measurement let you decline capital until a strategic reason appears.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether and when to raise capital, and how to operate while capital-light.

cards.title: Underwrite Fundraising From the Investor's Side
cards.summary: Understand the investor's money source, return target, and time horizon before pitching.
cards.use_when: Preparing a raise for an ecommerce or CPG brand and diagnosing why investor conversations stall.

cards.title: React to Unsolicited Diligence as a Seriousness Signal
cards.summary: Investors who do real research before a deal show conviction worth engaging.
cards.use_when: Evaluating inbound investor interest and deciding whether to take a meeting or engage with a buyer.

cards.title: Pivot When a Category TAM Is Shrinking
cards.summary: You cannot out-execute a shrinking addressable market; changing the bet can be the feat.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to keep investing in a category or brand whose market has plateaued.

cards.title: Pick the Right Mountain and Match It to Your Skills
cards.summary: Choosing what to work on is the biggest variable, and self-awareness is required to select it.
cards.use_when: Choosing which product line, category, or brand direction to commit your next quarters to.

cards.title: Build the Team Before the Big Bet
cards.summary: The source names picking the right co-founder as his best business decision.
cards.use_when: Choosing partners, co-founders, or key hires for a new brand launch or expansion.

cards.title: Master Humility as the Core CPG Founder Skill
cards.summary: The source names humility as the one skill every CPG founder needs.
cards.use_when: Operating a fast-growing brand and deciding how to react to feedback, data, and market signals.

cards.title: Reframe What Business Is For Beyond Money
cards.summary: The source's mature view is that business is about impact, team, and institution-building, not just money.
cards.use_when: Setting long-term goals for your brand and deciding exit versus long-term ownership.

cards.title: Solve an Emotional Problem, Not Just a Functional One
cards.summary: Position your product around an emotional need (comfort, anxiety relief) rather than a purely functional benefit to unlock a large addressable market.
cards.use_when: Deciding product positioning and messaging for a new or repositioning a product line, especially where the category has weak functional differentiation (e.g., apparel, hoodies).

cards.title: Reprice Down Fast When the Market Rejects Luxury Pricing
cards.summary: A new brand with no track record often can't command premium pricing, so test price downward quickly and commit once you find a range the market accepts.
cards.use_when: Launching or relaunching a product where you've priced it aspirational and the market is not converting (weak sell-through, cart abandonment, low conversion).

cards.title: Zero-Risk Affiliate Offer: Retainer Floor Plus Commission Upside
cards.summary: Structure creator affiliate deals as a guaranteed floor OR a commission rate (whichever is higher) to remove risk for new creators and snowball a network.
cards.use_when: Recruiting your first micro-creators or building a TikTok Shop affiliate network, especially when you have no track record to attract them on commission alone.

cards.title: Creative Velocity: Quality Through Quantity
cards.summary: Introduce a large volume of net-new creatives into ad accounts monthly, because you cannot predict which will win and volume accelerates learning.
cards.use_when: Scaling paid acquisition and diagnosing why ad performance has stalled — deciding how many new creatives to produce and test per month.

cards.title: Build an 80,000-Way UGC Format Library
cards.summary: Standardize a wide library of UGC formats so creators of different skill sets can produce content and you always have fresh creative angles.
cards.use_when: Briefing creators or planning UGC production, especially when some creators are strong on visuals but weak on camera presence.

cards.title: Recruit Micro-Creators and Customers as Affiliates
cards.summary: Recruit low-follower creators who feel a genuine connection to the brand — often your own customers — rather than paying large influencers.
cards.use_when: Sourcing affiliates when you have few or no creators yet, or deciding where to spend limited creator budget.

cards.title: Treat External Creators Like Internal Employees (Transparency Protocol)
cards.summary: Share real business data with top creators so they act with the brand's context and stay loyal — an employee-like relationship rather than a transactional one.
cards.use_when: Managing a creator/affiliate program at scale and deciding how much internal information to share to drive performance and retention.

cards.title: Promote Top Creators into Recruiters
cards.summary: Give your best-performing creators a small paid role to recruit and coach new creators, scaling the affiliate funnel beyond the founder.
cards.use_when: When founder-led creator recruitment becomes the bottleneck and you need the affiliate network to grow without you on every call.

cards.title: Scale Customer Support and Inventory Before Hyper-Growth Breaks Them
cards.summary: Rapid revenue spikes stress-test customer support and inventory; plan capacity and demand-suppression so growth doesn't break the business.
cards.use_when: Entering peak season or about to run a major promotion/drop, where a surge could overwhelm support or deplete inventory.

cards.title: Repurpose One Piece of Content Across Channels
cards.summary: Originate content once and distribute it across Meta, TikTok, Snapchat and Pinterest, paying creators commission on each channel it sells on.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to extend the life of winning UGC and whether/when to use creator whitelisting on paid channels.

cards.title: Use AI to Generate Hook Variations for Creator Testing
cards.summary: Feed proven hooks into an AI tool to generate large batches of hook variations, then have creators test them.
cards.use_when: When creative testing has stalled on hook angles and you need a large supply of new opening hooks.

cards.title: Plan for the Post-Sellout Capacity Crunch
cards.summary: A viral sell-out creates a supply and cash-flow hole; line up manufacturing lead time and continuity before you scale spend into a drop.
cards.use_when: Scheduling a launch/drop or scaling ad spend on a product with limited inventory.

cards.title: Adapting a Proven Creator Playbook to a New Category
cards.summary: Reuse the creators and channel knowledge from one product line to launch an adjacent category with a larger addressable market.
cards.use_when: Launching a second product line or category and deciding how to seed early momentum.

cards.title: Run Creator Management as an Employee-Style Org
cards.summary: Operate a network of hundreds of creators with the structure of an internal team — daily content quotas, hierarchy, and a small core staff.
cards.use_when: Scaling a creator program where you need output consistency and a way to manage hundreds of affiliates without hiring hundreds of staff.

cards.title: Treat Each Product/Color as a Distributable Revenue Stream
cards.summary: Frame every SKU, color and collection as a separate opportunity creators can promote, multiplying their earning potential and your content coverage.
cards.use_when: Managing a catalog of multiple products/colors and deciding how to merchandise them to affiliates and via paid channels.

cards.title: Diagnose the Inflection Point With Paid Ads and Creative Supply
cards.summary: When a brand starts scaling, the inflection usually comes from paid ads working plus a steady creative pipeline — verify both are in place before scaling spend.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to scale paid spend and diagnosing what is holding growth back.

cards.title: Set Clear Boundaries on A-List vs Micro Influencers
cards.summary: Celebrity and large-influencer audiences often don't convert; micro-creators and customers usually drive more revenue per dollar.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to spend on a celebrity or large-influencer partnership versus micro-creators and customers.

cards.title: Use Short-Form Organic Cold Traffic to Validate Before Paid
cards.summary: Prove demand through organic channel content (creator posts driving cold-traffic links) before committing to paid acquisition.
cards.use_when: Early-stage brands with no ad track record deciding where to grow first, or validating a new product.

cards.title: Build a Founder Support Network for Growth-Stage Problems
cards.summary: As you scale, problems become rarer and more extreme, so assemble a network of founders who have faced them before.
cards.use_when: When growth-stage operational problems (support, inventory, ad account structure) exceed what your team has experienced.

cards.title: Scale one SKU with product repositioning instead of new product launches
cards.summary: Grow ad spend on a single SKU by marketing it to many distinct personas and problem-solution angles rather than launching new physical products.
cards.use_when: Product selection and acquisition strategy when a single hero SKU has stalled in spend, or when deciding whether to launch a new product versus re-angle the existing one.

cards.title: Use LLMs as creative directors to generate 10-15 repositioning angles
cards.summary: Prompt an LLM to break one product into many non-generic direct-response angles, each with a distinct persona and logic mechanism.
cards.use_when: Acquisition creative planning when you need fresh ad angles but keep landing on generic audience labels.

cards.title: Target unexpected, specific personas instead of broad demographics
cards.summary: Shift new angle development from obvious demographic labels toward hyper-specific, logically motivated personas.
cards.use_when: Audience and messaging decisions when your angles are stuck on generic groups like 'toddler parents' and failing to stand out.

cards.title: Match repositioning ads to congruent custom landing pages
cards.summary: Route hyper-specific ad angles to pages dedicated to that exact persona, not a generic homepage or PDP.
cards.use_when: Landing-page and PDP decisions when running persona-specific acquisition ads across a single product.

cards.title: Map the product's benefit pillars onto audience demand
cards.summary: Identify all functional benefits of a multi-ingredient product, then build ad pillars so every audience finds the one benefit they care about.
cards.use_when: Messaging strategy when deciding which benefit pillars to advertise for a multi-benefit SKU.

cards.title: Diagnose spend saturation as an angle-TAM ceiling
cards.summary: Treat a stalled ad angle as a finite-TAM ceiling rather than a creative or bidding failure, and counter by adding new repositioning pillars.
cards.use_when: Ad-scaling decisions when a previously working angle stops absorbing more daily spend or frequency climbs.

cards.title: Choose repositioning over launches to protect cash flow and inventory
cards.summary: Adopt product repositioning as a lower-risk growth route when new product launches would strain cash, inventory and 3PL complexity.
cards.use_when: Product-portfolio and cash-flow decisions when considering adding SKUs to unlock more acquisition spend.

cards.title: Adapt repositioning to multi-SKU categories via SKU rotation
cards.summary: In categories with many products, rotate individual SKUs to new spend ceilings instead of repositioning one product.
cards.use_when: Acquisition scaling decisions for fashion, furniture or drop-ship catalogs with dozens or hundreds of SKUs.

cards.title: CAC-to-LTV and Payback Thresholds for Aggressive Scaling
cards.summary: IM8's scaling gate: 3.0-3.5x CAC:LTV on a 24-month horizon with blended payback under 4 months.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether your store's unit economics can support a spend increase, or setting the internal threshold before raising daily ad budget.

cards.title: Platform Mix for Scaling: 85/15 Meta to Google
cards.summary: IM8 allocates 85% of spend to Meta and 15% to Google while exploring podcasts, YouTube, AppLovin, TikTok and CTV.
cards.use_when: Setting or defending your paid acquisition channel allocation when planning a budget increase.

cards.title: Running 1,500 Concurrent Ads with a Daily Feedback Loop
cards.summary: High creative volume plus daily iteration is the operating system behind IM8's paid social scale.
cards.use_when: Building or auditing your ad creative production pipeline when paid social performance has plateaued.

cards.title: Shifting Production to AI-Generated Statics (75/25 Mix)
cards.summary: IM8 moved to 75% statics and 25% video, using AI for static generation, and reports 200M views from AI-generated video.
cards.use_when: Rebalancing your creative format mix to increase output speed and lower production cost.

cards.title: 3-Month Upfront Subscription to Lift AOV and Cash Flow
cards.summary: Pricing a 90-day upfront subscription at $235 versus $89/month raises IM8's global AOV to $280 and improves logistics.
cards.use_when: Designing or restructuring subscription plans, prepaid bundles, or billing cadence on a consumable product.

cards.title: Recognizing Revenue Upfront with Quarterly Billing
cards.summary: IM8's quarterly upfront billing lets a public company recognize subscription revenue immediately rather than over the term.
cards.use_when: Deciding subscription billing cadence when accounting treatment, cash timing or investor reporting matters to your store.

cards.title: Post-Purchase Value Stack: Masterclasses and VIP Access
cards.summary: IM8 retains 90-day subscribers by adding digital access to medical board masterclasses and celebrity trainer sessions.
cards.use_when: Improving retention or justifying a premium subscription tier by adding non-physical perks.

cards.title: Long-Term Equity Partnerships with Tier-1 Athletes
cards.summary: IM8 structures minimum 3-year equity deals with David Beckham and Sabalenka instead of transactional influencer payments.
cards.use_when: Negotiating a major creator or celebrity partnership and choosing between flat fees and equity or long-term alignment.

cards.title: Golden Ticket Experiences as a Wild-Bet Acquisition Hook
cards.summary: IM8 runs VIP giveaway experiences, such as trips to Dubai to meet Sabalenka, as high-attention acquisition and retention plays.
cards.use_when: Planning a promotional event or giveaway that needs to cut through paid social and drive both new customers and retention.

cards.title: Choosing DTC Over Retail to Protect Focus
cards.summary: IM8 runs 100% DTC (98% site, 2% Amazon), ships to 31 countries, and declines major retail offers to stay focused for three years.
cards.use_when: Evaluating a retail distribution offer or deciding whether to keep selling exclusively through your own store.
